rv.q: This glorious revival of William Finn and James Lapine's 1992. Tony winner about a Jewish family in the early 1980s is a masterpiece of musical theater storytelling.
There’s hardly a moment in the exhilarating, devastating revival of the musical “Falsettos” that doesn’t approach, or even achieve, perfection.
The show remains brave and hilarious, a charming and deeply moving treasure.
The revival is a triumph of thoughtful direction, superb performances and gorgeous singing that honors the material while giving it fresh emotional urgency.
This surprisingly fresh revival has been directed by original director Lapine, who plainly understands the bittersweet humor and provisional joy of that period.

"'March' is perhaps the more interesting half...The second act is more conventional...But it’s here that the work’s emotional heart beats most muscularly and anyone who leaves without shedding a tear may want to see his or her ophthalmologist...The Broadway revival is not a copy of the original...Neither is it a faultless work...
Few musicals have the range, idiosyncrasy and emotional punch of this profoundly unconventional and personal work.
You go because it reminds you that the world can change — and how, at great cost, it once did.

Mostly though, it is a unequivocal pleasure to let Finn's music and lyrics return to your consciousness — offering tales of the city that take us back but also remind us that family, as we define it for ourselves, remains our best defense against the horrors of life.
Not because this revival isn’t terrific — it is, mostly.

"So how does 'Falsettos' hold up...Better than 'The Normal Heart,' but not nearly so well as 'Angels in America'. The first act, 'March of the Falsettos,' remains impressive. Notwithstanding Finn’s inability to write once-heard-never-forgotten tunes, the musical numbers are cleverly crafted and the overall tone is appropriately tart...
Watching this revival of Falsettos on Broadway at the Theatre, one feels as though its time is now – more so even, than when it premiered in 1992.
This beautifully staged and performed revival is one of the most moving, eye and ear pleasing old-new musicals currently on Broadway.
This eloquent take bridges age and cultural boundaries and is as timeless as they come.
It is a mirror on life, as truthful and pure as only theatre can be.
Falsettos embraces all sexualities, new kinds of families, and all kinds of voices, without ever straying into preachiness.
The cast scores vocally, comically and dramatically, bringing out the manic heights and tender pauses of this truly extraordinary musical.
As a result, the evening shimmers and sparkles, and manages the curve its story serves us with honesty and enormous pathos.
Stephanie J. Block does a sensational job with Trina, who spends the show trying to be the grownup who can provide her son with a healthy, normal upbringing.
It’s an intimate sung-through musical that’s as smart and funny as it is life-affirming.
This revival of William Finn and James Lapine's musical about love, family, and loss in the age of AIDS is both heartbreaking and uplifting, with stellar performances across the board.
The time has never been riper for a revival of this beautiful show.
Just great--with only the merest reservations that certainly don't have anything to do with the several brilliant Finn songs.
This Falsettos makes a case for its inclusion in the classic musical canon.
Curse you, William Finn, for writing these heart-wrenching songs.
Plan on being deeply touched and richly satisfied at this show.
I’m glad I saw Falsettos in its current iteration and find it a period piece with enormous vitality.
Forget the title: Falsettos might just be the deepest musical in town.
This near-perfect revival of a decidedly imperfect musical tells that story quite well.

"Offers plenty to admire even if it never fully coheres or proves as affecting as it wants to be...Lapine directed this revival and my guess is that 'Falsettos' ultimately needed someone not quite so close to the material to make it resonate fully with a contemporary audience...
But ultimately I found “Falsettos” neither terrible nor terrific, and that surprised me.
Finn and Lapine put the “false” in “Falsettos.”
That’s what it is like experiencing Finn’s work, with melodies and words that are smart and moving, quirky and personal and honest.
Even after 25 years, William Finn’s melodic Falsettos continues to explore the many sides of family with its exuberant joy, love and heartbreaking loss.
It's more like a 'really nice' than a transformative 'OMG,' but still, all these years later, 'Falsettos' still deserves high-pitched praise.

The music in Falsettos is gorgeous and fun, complex and surprising, and with a show aimed at exploring sexuality, alternative families, and AIDS, it doesn’t, even to this day, seem to handle these in traditional or melodramatic ways.

The musical makes an unintended statement about what attitudes should have been back then, in what they seem to be today. Finn's music ranges from fun to moving (there were a lot of tears shed at the end of act one) and the lyrics are touching: Whizzer: Lets get on with living while we can And not play dumb.
The cast is a thoroughly winsome one, which compensates for the first act becoming at points a bit repetitious once the basic situation is set.
As far as 35-year-old rom-com setups go, this one does not retain much impact.
But it just doesn't click for me as a musical.
While I enjoyed the overall performance, it left me with a feeling of being incomplete, unexplained at times, and disjointed.
This is a triple AAA perfectly selected cast that leaves you grappling with every emotion imaginable in this newly refreshed revival that never tires.
This outstanding production never feels dated.
Falsettos shines just as brightly in 2016.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this revival as fresh and emotionally devastating, praising the stellar cast and Finn's distinctive score. Some find the first act repetitive and the sentimentality cloying, but most laud its humor, humanity, and heartbreaking power.
